summary: Defines a Uniform Resource Name namespace for UUIDs (also called GUIDs), 128-bit identifiers that can be generated without central coordination and are meant to be unique across space and time. The format comes from the Apollo and DCE systems and was later used on Microsoft Windows. It was replaced by RFC 9562.

eli5.summary: Imagine giving every grain of sand its own name tag, made up so cleverly that no two tags ever match, even if nobody compares notes. A UUID is that kind of tag for computer things.

questions: how is a version 1 uuid generated
subtitle: How to make a 128-bit identifier that is unique everywhere without asking anyone for permission.

tldr.problem: Systems need identifiers that are unique across space and time, but a central authority handing them out is slow and a bottleneck.
tldr.mechanism: A UUID is a 128-bit value built from a timestamp and MAC address, from a hash of a name, or from random numbers. This RFC also registers the UUID namespace for URNs.
tldr.outcome: UUIDs can be generated on demand with no registration. This RFC has been replaced by RFC 9562.

today: RFC 4122 is obsoleted by RFC 9562, which is now the definition of UUIDs. Read this RFC for its history; use the newer one for current work.

sections.title: Why UUIDs Exist
sections.content:
A UUID (Universally Unique IDentifier, also called a GUID) is 128 bits long and requires no central registration process. Because no central authority is needed, generation on demand can be completely automated. The RFC says the algorithm supports allocation rates of up to 10 million per second per machine if necessary.

The fixed 128-bit size is small compared to the alternatives, which suits sorting, hashing and storing in databases. Since a new UUID needs no registration, UUIDs are among the URNs with the lowest minting cost.
sections.eli5: Normally a teacher hands out student numbers so nobody gets the same one. UUIDs let every kid make their own number without asking, and still never clash.

sections.title: The URN Namespace and String Form
sections.content:
Section 3 is the registration template for the UUID namespace ID, declared by JTC 1/SC6 (ASN.1 Rapporteur Group). Each field is printed as a zero-filled hexadecimal string, most significant digit first. Lowercase letters are output, and input is case insensitive.

The string has five dash-separated groups: time-low, time-mid, time-high-and-version, the clock sequence fields, and a 6-octet node. The RFC's example is urn:uuid:f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6.

Two UUIDs are equal if and only if all corresponding fields are equal. UUIDs are not globally resolvable, so resolution does not apply, and the only validity check is whether the timestamp is in the future.
sections.eli5: A UUID is written as a row of numbers and letters split by dashes, like a long serial number on a toy box. Two serial numbers are the same only if every part matches.

sections.title: The UUID Layout
sections.content:
A UUID is 16 octets. It is defined as fields that are whole numbers of octets, most significant byte first (network byte order): time_low (octets 0-3), time_mid (4-5), time_hi_and_version (6-7), clock_seq_hi_and_reserved (8), clock_seq_low (9) and node (10-15).

The variant field, in the top bits of octet 8, decides the layout. This document specifies the variant whose first two bits are 1 and 0. The version sits in the most significant 4 bits of time_hi_and_version: 1 is time-based, 2 is DCE Security, 3 is name-based with MD5, 4 is random, and 5 is name-based with SHA-1.

The nil UUID has all 128 bits set to zero.
sections.eli5: A UUID is like a form with labelled boxes. One box says which kind of UUID it is, and the other boxes hold time, a counter and a machine number, or just random digits.

sections.title: Three Ways to Make a UUID
sections.content:
Time-based (version 1). The timestamp is a 60-bit count of 100-nanosecond intervals since 00:00:00.00, 15 October 1582. The node is an IEEE 802 MAC address. A clock sequence guards against duplicates when the clock is set backwards or the node ID changes; it MUST be initialized once to a random number and MUST NOT be correlated to the node identifier. If a system requests too many UUIDs within one clock tick, the generator MUST return an error or stall.

Name-based (versions 3 and 5). Hash a name space ID concatenated with the name, using MD5 or SHA-1 (SHA-1 is preferred if backward compatibility is not an issue), then copy hash octets into the fields and set the version and variant bits. The same name in the same name space MUST always give the same UUID.

Random (version 4). Set the version and variant bits and make all other bits random or pseudo-random.

If no MAC address is available or its use is undesirable, section 4.5 suggests a 47-bit cryptographic-quality random node ID with the multicast bit set to one, so it can never clash with a real network card address.
sections.eli5: You can build a UUID from the clock plus your machine's number, from scrambling a name the same way every time, or by rolling lots of dice. All three give a tag nobody else should have.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns not to assume UUIDs are hard to guess. They should not be used as security capabilities, meaning identifiers whose mere possession grants access. A predictable random number source makes this worse.

People also cannot easily tell by eye whether a UUID has been slightly altered to redirect a reference. Applications that generate UUIDs on many hosts must be willing to rely on the random number source at every host; if that is not feasible, the name-based approach should be used.
sections.eli5: A UUID is a name tag, not a secret password. Do not let anyone in just because they know the tag.
